title: Stage Presence Without Performance
hook: The speakers people trust are rarely the most theatrical; they are the ones whose bodies look like they belong to the person talking.
why:
Sooner or later, most working lives involve standing up in front of people: a presentation to a team, a talk at a conference, a speech at a wedding, a eulogy. For many men it is one of the most dreaded moments of their year. The advice they find tends to be about technique: where to put your hands, how to stand, how many steps to take, when to make eye contact. Much of it produces speakers who look like they are following instructions.

This chapter takes a different view. Presence on a stage is less about performing confidence than about letting your body do what it does naturally when you care about what you are saying, without the interference of fear. It covers how common the fear really is, why your nerves show less than you think, how to reframe the racing heart, why gestures help you think, how to move with purpose, what to do with a lectern and a pause, and how to look at a room. The aim is a speaker whose body looks like it belongs to the person talking, not a performance laid on top of him.

teach.h: The fear is common, but not what you have heard.
teach.p:
It is often said that people fear public speaking more than death. The comedian Jerry Seinfeld built a joke on it: at a funeral, the average person would rather be in the coffin than giving the eulogy. The claim goes back to a survey from 1973, and it is repeated in countless books and courses.

In 2012 Karen Dwyer and Marlina Davidson looked into it. They gave 815 American college students a list of fears and asked them to choose the ones they feared most. Speaking before a group was chosen more often than any other fear, including death. But when the students were asked to rank their fears, death came first. Public speaking is a very common fear, then, but not usually a greater one than dying. The famous claim depended on how the question was asked.

The correction matters, because exaggerated claims about the fear tend to feed it. If you have been told that public speaking is the most terrifying thing people do, your nerves before a talk seem to confirm that something awful is coming. In fact the fear is ordinary, shared by most people in the audience, and usually fades quickly once you start.

The fear also shows in the body in predictable ways. Breathing moves up into the chest and becomes fast and shallow, the shoulders rise, the hands go cold, and the voice may tighten. The figure here breathes high in the chest, the pattern of a body bracing for threat. Knowing what the body is doing is the first step to working with it rather than against it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people consistently ranked public speaking as a greater fear than death. In Dwyer and Davidson's survey, it was chosen most often from a list, but death came first when students ranked their fears.

teach.h: Your nerves show less than you think.
teach.p:
Part VI described the illusion of transparency: people believe their inner states are far more visible to others than they really are. The speaker with a pounding heart assumes the audience can see it. Usually they cannot. Most of what a nervous speaker feels, from the racing heart to the churning stomach to the sense of the mind going blank, is invisible from the seats.

In 2003 Kenneth Savitsky and Thomas Gilovich tested whether knowing this helps. Students gave a short, unprepared speech in front of an audience. Some were simply told to relax. Others were told about the illusion of transparency: that people's nerves are usually much less visible than they feel. Those who were told about the illusion felt less nervous, rated their own speeches more favourably, and were rated as better speakers by the people watching.

The mechanism seems to be a spiral that the knowledge interrupts. A speaker who believes his nerves are visible becomes more anxious about being seen as anxious, which makes the nerves worse. A speaker who knows that his nerves are mostly private can let them be, and they are less likely to build.

This is not a promise that nobody will notice anything. A trembling hand on a sheet of paper or a shaky voice in the first sentence may show. But the audience tends to forget these quickly, and most are sympathetic: they would be nervous too. The figure here stands simply, weight even, hands loose. That is roughly what a nervous speaker looks like from the audience, whatever is happening inside.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if telling speakers about the illusion of transparency made no difference to their performance. In Savitsky and Gilovich's study, it reduced their nerves and improved how observers rated their speeches.
teach.pullQuote: Most of what a nervous speaker feels is invisible from the seats.

teach.p:
The usual advice to nervous speakers is to calm down. The trouble is that calming down is hard to do on command, especially when your heart is racing and the talk starts in two minutes. Trying and failing can make things worse.

In 2014 Alison Wood Brooks tried a different approach. Before performing in front of others, including giving a short persuasive speech on camera, people were asked to say either I am calm or I am excited. Those who said I am excited gave speeches that independent viewers rated as more persuasive, more competent and more confident, and they spoke for longer. They did not necessarily feel less anxious. What changed was how they interpreted the arousal and what they did with it.

The idea is that anxiety and excitement feel physically similar: a fast heart, alert senses, energy. Calling it anxiety frames the moment as a threat, which pulls attention towards what might go wrong. Calling it excitement frames it as an opportunity, which pulls attention towards what you want to say. Part VI's chapter on reading yourself under stress mentioned this study. Here it becomes something to do in the wings.

Pair the reappraisal with the body. A slow breath that moves the belly rather than the chest, with a long exhale, settles some of the physical alarm without fighting it. The chapter on breath in Part II explains why. The figure here breathes low, the belly rising, shoulders down. Say I am excited, take two slow breaths like this, and walk on.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if saying I am excited before a speech made no difference to how it was received. In Brooks's study, it led to speeches rated as more persuasive, competent and confident than those given after saying I am calm.

teach.p:
Many speakers are told what to do with their hands, and the advice usually involves controlling them: keep them still, keep them at your sides, hold a pen, use this gesture for this point. Research on gesture suggests that this misunderstands what hands are for.

In 2001 Susan Goldin-Meadow and her colleagues asked children and adults to explain how they had solved a maths problem while also holding a list of words or letters in memory. Sometimes they were free to gesture while explaining, and sometimes they were asked to keep their hands still. When they could gesture, they remembered more of the list. The researchers concluded that gesturing lightened the mental load of explaining, freeing capacity for other things.

For a speaker, this suggests that gestures are not decoration added to speech but part of how speech is produced. A speaker whose hands are pinned to his sides, or rigidly following a script of planned movements, is using some of his mind to restrain or direct his hands, and has less left for thinking. The result is often a stiffer delivery and a more frequent sense of losing the thread.

The practical lesson is to free the hands rather than to choreograph them. Do not hold anything you do not need. Start with the hands loose and in front of you, roughly at waist height, where they can move easily. Then let them do what they do when you are explaining something to a friend. If you watch a recording later and find a gesture repeated to distraction, that is worth adjusting. But begin by letting go. The figure here presents with an open, explaining hand, the gesture that comes naturally when someone is thinking aloud for others.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if keeping the hands still while explaining had no cost. In Goldin-Meadow's study, people remembered less when they could not gesture, which suggests that gesture supports thinking while speaking.

teach.p:
Movement on a stage can help or distract, and the difference is mostly about purpose. A speaker who paces back and forth, or rocks from foot to foot, is usually discharging nervous energy. The audience's eyes follow the movement, and the words become harder to attend to. A speaker who never moves at all can seem frozen, especially on a large stage.

A useful principle is to move on transitions and stand still on points. When you shift from one section of a talk to the next, a few steps to a new position marks the change, as a new paragraph does on a page. When you reach something important, stop, plant your feet and say it. Stillness at the key moment makes it land.

This also helps the nervous speaker. Walking during a transition uses some of the restless energy, and planting the feet afterwards gives a sense of solidity. Weight evenly on both feet, knees soft rather than locked, is a stance that can be held comfortably for a long time.

Not every setting allows movement. A small meeting room, a video talk or a wedding speech from a fixed spot may keep you in one place. Then the same principle applies on a smaller scale: a shift of weight or a turn of the body towards a different part of the room can mark a transition, and stillness still marks the point. The figure here walks across a stage between sections of a talk, purposeful rather than restless. When he reaches the next spot, he will stop before he speaks.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if audiences found constant pacing as easy to follow as purposeful movement and stillness. Most speakers who review recordings of themselves find that restless movement pulls attention away from the words.

teach.p:
A lectern is useful. It holds your notes, it gives your hands somewhere to rest, and for a nervous speaker it can feel like a shelter. That is also its problem. Gripped with both hands for a whole talk, it becomes a barrier between speaker and audience, and the speaker's body disappears behind it except for a head and a pair of white knuckles.

If you use a lectern, use it lightly. Rest your notes on it and stand slightly to one side, or step out from behind it for a story or a key point and return when you need your notes. Let your hands leave it to gesture. In many rooms, simply stepping beside it changes how close the audience feels to you.

The other tool most nervous speakers underuse is the pause. Anxiety speeds speech up, and fast speakers often fill every gap with um and so, afraid that silence will look like failure. In fact a pause of two or three seconds rarely feels long to an audience. Before an important point, it creates anticipation. After one, it gives people time to take it in. A pause also gives you a moment to breathe and find the next thought.

A useful practice is to pause deliberately at the end of each section and before each key sentence, even if it feels too long. Recording a rehearsal and listening back usually shows that the pauses that felt endless sounded natural. The figure here stands at a lectern, notes in front of him. Whether it becomes a support or a shield depends on how tightly he holds it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if audiences experienced short pauses as awkward failures. Most speakers who listen to recordings find that pauses which felt long sound natural, and that the points after them land more clearly.

teach.h: A room is a series of people.
teach.p:
Eye contact with an audience is often taught as a technique: scan the room, look at the back wall, divide the room into zones. These can help, but they can also produce the glazed, sweeping look of someone following a rule. A better approach is to treat the room as a series of people.

Speak each thought, or each sentence, to one person, and hold their eyes until the thought is finished. Then move to someone in a different part of the room for the next thought. This is closer to how conversation works, and each person you look at feels spoken to. The rest of the room, watching you speak to one of them, feels it too. In a large hall, where individual faces blur, look at small groups in turn in the same way.

This connects to the deeper point of this chapter. Audiences trust speakers who seem to be themselves. A naturally quiet man who tries to perform the big gestures and booming voice of a motivational speaker usually looks uncomfortable, because his body is acting out a role that is not his. The same man speaking at his own pace, with his own gestures, about something he cares about, is often far more compelling. Presence is not volume. It is congruence: words, voice and body all coming from the same person.

The techniques in this chapter, reframing nerves, freeing the hands, moving with purpose, pausing and looking at people, are not a performance to be layered on top. They remove the interference that stops your own manner from showing. The figure here gestures openly towards the audience, speaking to someone in particular.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if audiences consistently preferred theatrical delivery to a speaker's natural manner. Speakers who imitate a style that is not their own often look uncomfortable, and audiences tend to notice the mismatch.
teach.pullQuote: Presence is not volume. It is words, voice and body all coming from the same person.

poseGallery.doCaption: Low, slow breaths before walking on
poseGallery.dontCaption: Breathing high and fast in the wings
poseGallery.annotation: You cannot order yourself to calm down, but two slow belly breaths and the words I am excited change what the arousal does.
Restrained hands cost mental effort. Let them move as they would if you were explaining something to a friend.
Move on transitions and stand still on points. Stillness at the important moment makes it land.
A lectern held tightly becomes a shield. Step beside it, or out from behind it, when you want the audience closer.

poseGallery.doCaption: Facing the room, the slide behind
poseGallery.dontCaption: Back to the audience, reading the slide
poseGallery.annotation: The audience looks where you look. Turn to the slide to point, then turn back before you speak about it.

poseGallery.doCaption: Hands loose, a breath out, then the first line
poseGallery.dontCaption: Tugging at the collar before you begin
poseGallery.annotation: Fidgeting before a talk feeds the nerves. Let your hands hang loose and breathe out slowly before you walk on.

caseStudy:
Kwame, twenty-nine, a data analyst, was asked to give a twenty-minute talk at an industry conference about a project his team had led. He had never spoken to more than a dozen people. He watched videos of famous speakers, wrote out his talk word for word, and practised in front of a mirror with planned gestures: an open palm here, a sweep of the arm there, three steps to the left at the end of the introduction.

In the first rehearsal with his team, it went badly. He forgot a planned gesture, lost his place in the script, and froze. A colleague who had spoken at conferences watched him and said he looked like he was doing an impression of someone else.

Kwame changed his approach. He turned the script into a single page of headings. He stopped planning gestures and simply explained the project to his colleague, as he would over coffee, while she watched his hands. They moved on their own, and his explanation was clearer than the script. He kept just two pieces of staging: a few steps between each section, and a pause before the main finding.

On the day, his heart was pounding in the wings. He told himself he was excited, which felt silly, and took two slow breaths. In the first minute his voice wavered, and he was sure everyone could hear it. Nobody mentioned it afterwards. Halfway through, he caught himself speaking each point to one face in the third row, then another by the window, and realised he had stopped thinking about the audience as a crowd.

Several people came to talk to him afterwards. None of them commented on his delivery. They wanted to know more about the project, which he decided was the best review he could have had.
observe: Notice where your breath sits in the minutes before you speak in front of others, and what your shoulders are doing.
Notice what your hands do when you explain something to a friend, without thinking about it.
Notice, in a talk you attend, whether the speaker's movement marks transitions or simply discharges nerves.
Notice how long a pause feels when you make one and how long it seems when someone else does.

drills.name: Explain It to a Friend
steps: Choose a topic you will need to present soon.
Explain it to a friend or partner for five minutes, without notes, as you would over coffee.
Ask them to watch your hands, posture and eyes rather than the content.
Ask what looked most natural, and what disappeared when you got interested.
Use that as the starting point for your delivery, rather than a planned set of gestures.
variations: Explain the same topic to two different friends, one who knows the subject and one who does not, and notice how your hands change.
Record yourself explaining the topic to a friend, then watch the recording with the sound off and note which gestures carried the meaning.
Ask your friend to interrupt you once with a question, and notice how you recover your thread without notes.

drills.name: Wings Routine
steps: Before your next talk or presentation, find a quiet spot a few minutes before you start.
Say I am excited, out loud if you can, or under your breath if not.
Take two or three slow breaths into the belly, with a long exhale.
Let your shoulders drop and your hands hang loose.
Walk on and pause for a breath before your first sentence.
variations: Try the routine before a small, low-stakes moment, such as speaking up in a meeting, so that it is familiar by the time you need it on a stage.
Try a version of the routine before a phone call or a video call, adapted to where you are, and notice whether your opening is steadier.
Pair the routine with walking the stage or the room beforehand, if you can, and notice whether the two together help more than either alone.

drills.name: Pause Practice
steps: Record yourself giving the first three minutes of a talk.
Mark each section break and each key sentence on your notes.
Record it again, pausing for two or three seconds at each mark.
Listen to both and note which sounds clearer and more confident.
variations: Practise pausing after a question in an ordinary conversation, counting two seconds before you answer, and notice how the other person responds.
Mark the one sentence in your talk that matters most, and practise a three-second pause before and after it.
Ask a friend to time your pauses during a rehearsal, and compare their times with how long the pauses felt to you.

drills.name: One Person per Thought
steps: In your next meeting or presentation, speak each point to one person and hold their eyes until the point is finished.
Move to someone in a different part of the room for the next point.
Notice whether people respond differently when you speak to them directly.
Afterwards, note whether you felt more or less nervous than usual.
variations: In a large room, practise speaking each thought to a small group in turn, rather than to one face, and notice whether the room feels smaller.
During questions, practise beginning each answer to the questioner and ending it by looking back at them.
In a one-to-one conversation, notice how you naturally hold someone's eyes until a thought is finished, and bring that rhythm to your next talk.

quiz.q: A colleague says that people fear public speaking more than death, so your nerves before a talk are only natural. What did Dwyer and Davidson find?
options: Public speaking was chosen most often from a list, but death came first when fears were ranked
Public speaking was ranked as the single greatest fear above death by nearly every student surveyed
Very few students feared public speaking at all, once they had taken a course on how to do it
Fear of death and fear of public speaking turned out to be the same fear, measured in two ways
quiz.explain: The famous claim depended on how the question was asked. Public speaking is a very common fear, but when students ranked their fears, death came first.

quiz.q: In Savitsky and Gilovich's study, what happened when speakers were told about the illusion of transparency?
options: They became more anxious, because they started watching for signs of their own nerves
They felt less nervous and were rated by observers as giving better speeches
They felt the same as before, but observers noticed their nerves much less
Nothing changed, because knowing about a bias does not alter how it works
quiz.explain: Knowing that their nerves were less visible than they felt seemed to interrupt the spiral of worrying about looking nervous. Observers rated their speeches more favourably.

quiz.q: In Brooks's study, what did saying I am excited before a speech change?
options: It made people feel completely calm, which is why their speeches improved
It made speeches shorter and more focused, because people wanted to finish quickly
It had no effect on the speech itself, only on how people felt about it afterwards
Speeches were rated more persuasive and confident, though anxiety was not necessarily lower
quiz.explain: Reappraising arousal as excitement changed what people did with it, not necessarily how anxious they felt. Independent viewers rated their speeches as more persuasive, competent and confident.

quiz.q: What did Goldin-Meadow and her colleagues find when people explained a maths problem with and without gesturing?
options: Gesturing distracted them, so they remembered less of a word list held in mind
Gesturing had no effect on memory, though it did make explanations longer
When they could gesture, they remembered more of a list held in memory
Only children benefited from gesturing; adults did better with still hands
quiz.explain: Gesturing seemed to lighten the mental load of explaining, freeing capacity for remembering. Pinning the hands still, or scripting them, uses some of that capacity.

quiz.q: You are about to give an important presentation and your heart is pounding. What fits this chapter best?
options: Tell yourself you are excited, breathe slowly, and remember that most of it will not show
Tell yourself firmly to calm down, and do not begin until you feel completely relaxed
Apologise to the audience for your nerves at the start, so that they make allowances
Grip the lectern with both hands for the whole talk, so that nobody can see you shake
quiz.explain: Reappraisal, slow breathing and the knowledge that nerves are less visible than they feel all have support. Waiting to feel calm, or hiding behind the lectern, tends to make things worse.

quiz.q: A friend preparing a wedding speech has planned a gesture for every line. What advice fits this chapter best?
options: Keep the plan, because audiences remember gestures far more than they remember any words
Practise telling the stories to someone, and let the hands do what they naturally do
Drop all gestures and keep the hands at the sides, so nothing distracts from the words
Copy the gestures of a well-known speaker, since those have already been proven to work
quiz.explain: Scripted gestures tend to look like a performance and use up mental effort. Gestures that arise naturally while explaining are part of how speech is produced, and they look like they belong to the speaker.

quiz.q: What principle does this chapter suggest for moving around a stage?
options: Keep moving throughout the talk, so that the audience never has time to lose interest in you
Move on transitions between sections, and stand still for the key points you want to land
Stay completely still from start to finish, since any movement at all distracts an audience
Walk towards the person who seems least interested, so that they feel obliged to pay attention
quiz.explain: Movement on a transition marks a change, as a new paragraph does on a page. Stillness on a key point makes it land, and walking between sections uses some restless energy.

quiz.q: Three minutes into your talk, the projector fails. What fits this chapter best?
options: Stop and wait in silence until the technician has fixed it, however long that takes
Step towards the audience and carry on, letting your words and hands carry the content
Apologise at length for the problem, so that the audience knows it was not your fault
Abandon the talk, since without slides the audience will not follow the argument
quiz.explain: A talk that has been rehearsed aloud lives in the speaker, not the slides. Carrying on, with free hands to sketch what the slides would have shown, often makes the moment memorable rather than disastrous.

quiz.q: Someone advises starting every talk by telling the audience how nervous you are, so that they will be sympathetic. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That announcing nerves draws the audience's attention to feelings that were mostly invisible to them
That audiences can always see a speaker's nerves, so it is best to admit them straight away
That announcing nerves is the most effective way to calm your own heart rate before speaking
That audiences rate nervous speakers more highly whenever the nerves are openly acknowledged
quiz.explain: Because of the illusion of transparency, most of what a nervous speaker feels is invisible from the seats. Announcing it makes people look for it, and frames the talk as an ordeal.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific time you spoke in front of a group: a presentation, a speech, a toast or a eulogy. Describe what your body did in the minutes before and the first minute after you started: your breath, your hands, your voice. What did you believe the audience could see? Having read this chapter, which one change, to how you frame the nerves, how you use your hands, how you move or how you pause, would you try next time, and why?
reflection.guidance: Most people remember speaking moments vividly and judge them harshly. Try to separate what you felt from what the audience could actually have seen. Be specific about one change rather than a list, and choose the one that addresses whatever got in the way of your natural manner.

failureMode: The first failure is to believe your nerves are as visible as they feel, and to let that belief make them worse. The second is to try to force yourself to calm down, when reframing the arousal as excitement works better. The third is to pin your hands or script your gestures, when free hands support thinking. The fourth is to pace to burn off nerves, when movement should mark transitions and stillness should mark points. The fifth is to hide behind a lectern or rush past every pause. And the sixth is to imitate a theatrical speaker whose manner is not yours, when audiences trust a body that looks like it belongs to the person talking.

moreCases.title: The best man who raced
moreCases.scene:
Sam, thirty-one, is best man at his oldest friend's wedding. He has written a good speech: three stories from their school days, a touching paragraph about the bride, and a toast. He has timed it at six minutes. He has practised it in his head on the train every morning for a fortnight, but never out loud, because his flatmates would hear.

At the reception, he stands up in front of a hundred and twenty guests with the speech on four cards. His heart is hammering and his mouth is dry. He starts reading at once, before the room has quite settled, and goes faster and faster. The first story's punchline arrives before anyone has understood the set-up, and only a few people laugh. He hears the thin laughter and speeds up further, to get to the next story. He finishes in just under three minutes, raises his glass and sits down.

The groom hugs him. The bride's father says, kindly, that it was very good. Sam is sure it was a disaster.

Later, the groom's grandmother, who is hard of hearing, asks him what the story about the school trip was, because she missed it. He tells it to her at the table, slowly, and she laughs so much she has to put her glass down.

The groom had asked him to keep it short, which Sam had taken to mean that it should be over as quickly as possible. What the groom had meant was no more than ten minutes.

His flatmate, who was at the wedding, tells him the next morning that the speech was nice but that nobody could keep up, and that the bride's mother had leaned over during the second story and asked what had happened to the tent.

He had also decided to read the cards rather than look up, because he was afraid that if he caught anyone's eye he would lose his place.
moreCases.misread:
Sam read the thin laughter as proof that his stories were not funny, and sped up to escape. The guests, many of whom had missed the set-ups, read the speech as nervous and rushed, though warm. Nobody but Sam read it as a disaster.

And he read the bride's father's "very good" as pity, when it was what fathers of brides say about every speech, and meant kindly.

The guests who laughed thinly were mostly laughing at the bits they had caught. A slower telling would have given the rest of the room the chance to catch up, and the laugh would have grown.
moreCases.betterRead:
Anxiety speeds speech up, and fast speakers leave the audience no time to catch up. Jokes need a pause after the set-up and another after the punchline, and a room of a hundred and twenty people needs more time than a table of six. Sam's stories were funny, as his telling at the table proved. What failed was the pace. His better approach, which he used at his brother's wedding two years later, began with practising aloud, standing, at least five times. He waited for the room to settle before his first word. He paused after each set-up and let each laugh finish before going on. He told himself, as he stood up, that he was excited, which made him laugh at himself and helped. The speech ran seven minutes, and his brother's new wife asked him for a copy.

He also asked the groom's grandmother to sit near the front, and told the school-trip story to her, which made the whole room lean in.

moreCases.title: The quiet scientist on the course
moreCases.scene:
Tomasz, forty-five, is a research chemist, quiet, precise and well respected in his field. His company sends him on a two-day presentation course before he gives the keynote at a customer conference. The trainer, an energetic former actor, tells the group that great speakers own the stage. He has them practise striding to the front, booming their opening line, opening their arms wide and pausing for effect. He tells Tomasz that he is too still and too soft, and that he needs to "bring the energy".

Tomasz does his best. At the conference, he strides on, opens his arms and booms his first line, which is a joke the trainer suggested. Several people laugh politely. For the next twenty minutes he works hard at the big gestures and the big voice. It is exhausting, and it shows. His colleagues, who know him well, watch with discomfort.

In the feedback forms, the customers rate the content highly. Several comments say the speaker seemed uncomfortable, and one says he seemed to be "acting the part of a presenter". Another says that the most convincing moment was during the questions, when he forgot about the stage, stood still and explained the chemistry in his own quiet way.

Tomasz reads the forms and feels foolish. His manager, Ines, says that she thinks the problem was the course, not him.

The trainer filmed each participant on the first day and played the clips back to the group, pausing on Tomasz's to point out that his hands barely moved. Tomasz had not wanted to say that he had been concentrating on what he was saying.

On the second day the trainer praised him warmly for a big, sweeping gesture during a practice run. Tomasz had not meant it; he had been reaching for his water.

Ines had sat through the keynote in the second row. She tells him that she could see him working, and that watching someone work that hard at being relaxed is tiring for the audience too.
moreCases.misread:
The trainer read Tomasz's stillness and quiet voice as weaknesses to be fixed. Tomasz read the trainer's advice as the right way to present and his own manner as a deficiency. The customers read the performance as someone acting a part.

The trainer had read a single style of presence as the only one, and assumed that a quiet speaker must be a weak one.

His colleagues read his discomfort accurately, but nobody had told him before the conference that the course might not suit him, because the course had been everyone's idea.
moreCases.betterRead:
Audiences tend to trust a body that looks as though it belongs to the person talking. A quiet man performing the big gestures and booming voice of a showman usually looks uncomfortable, because his body is acting out a role, and audiences notice the gap. Tomasz's natural manner, still, precise and attentive, was exactly what made his answers during the questions convincing. His better approach, which Ines helped him plan for the next conference, was to keep that manner and add only what supported it: a few steps between sections, a pause before each key finding, each point spoken to one person in the room, and his hands free to explain the chemistry as they did over coffee. He kept his voice at its natural level and used a good microphone. The feedback the next year called him "clear", "credible" and, to his surprise, "engaging".

He also stopped opening with a joke. He opened instead with a question his customers had asked him, which got their attention without anyone having to laugh.

moreCases.title: The student who apologised for her nerves
moreCases.scene:
Amara, twenty-two, is a final-year nursing student, and she has to present a case to a meeting of the ward team: two consultants, a ward manager, several nurses and some medical students. She knows the patient and the case well. She has prepared her slides carefully. She has also barely slept, and when she stands up, her hands are shaking and her voice wobbles on the first sentence.

She stops and says, "Sorry, I'm really nervous." A few people smile encouragingly. She starts again, wobbles again, and says, "Sorry, I'm so sorry, I'm just really nervous." By the third apology, the room has gone very quiet, and the ward manager says gently, "Take your time." Amara feels as though every person in the room is watching her shake.

She gets through the presentation, and the content is good, but she is mortified. She is sure that everyone saw how frightened she was, and that the consultants now think she cannot cope under pressure.

The next day, one of the consultants stops her in the corridor and says that her analysis of the patient's medication was the best he had heard from a student that year. He does not mention the nerves. When she does, he looks puzzled and says he had thought the apologies were just politeness.

She had rehearsed the presentation twice in her room, sitting on the bed, reading from her laptop. She had not practised standing up, or speaking to anyone, or what she would do with her hands.

Afterwards, a medical student who had presented the week before tells her that he had been terrified too, and that he had watched her the whole time thinking how calm she looked until she said she was nervous.

That evening she writes in her reflective journal that she must learn to be less nervous, and underlines it twice.
moreCases.misread:
Amara read her own nerves as obvious to everyone and assumed the consultants had judged her by them. By apologising, she drew the room's attention to the nerves, which most people had barely noticed until she named them.

And she read the ward manager's "Take your time" as a sign that her nerves were obvious, when it was a response to her apologies.

The medical students, who had all presented before, mostly read her shaking as ordinary, the way everyone feels at a first case presentation. The apologies were the part they remembered.
moreCases.betterRead:
Savitsky and Gilovich found that speakers who were told about the illusion of transparency, that nerves are much less visible than they feel, felt calmer and were rated as better speakers by the people watching. Amara's shaking hands and wobbling voice were real, but far less visible from the seats than from inside her body, and the consultant had barely noticed them. Repeated apologies turned an invisible feeling into a visible topic. Her better approach, which a tutor suggested, was to say nothing about the nerves, take a slow breath out, pause after the first sentence, rest her hands on the table or the lectern for a moment if they shook, and carry on. At her next case presentation, she did exactly that. Her voice wobbled once and steadied. Nobody mentioned it, including her.

She also stopped rehearsing on her bed. She practised her next presentation standing in the empty seminar room, aloud, twice, with a friend pretending to be a consultant.

moreCases.title: The manager behind the lectern
moreCases.scene:
Ravi, fifty, manages a food processing plant that employs three hundred people. Head office has decided to close one of the plant's two production lines, and ninety jobs will go. Ravi has to tell the workforce at a meeting in the dispatch hall at six in the morning, between shifts. He has a statement drafted by head office and a list of support arrangements. The hall has a temporary lectern and a microphone.

He stands behind the lectern, grips it with both hands, and reads the statement word for word, looking down. It takes four minutes. He looks up only at the end, when he says that he will take questions. There is a long silence. Someone at the back shouts that he does not even have the guts to look at them. Ravi feels his face go hot and reads the support arrangements, again looking down.

He has worked at the plant for twenty-two years, and he knows many of the people in the hall by name. He had fought the decision for months and lost. Almost nobody in the hall knows that.

That afternoon, the union representative, Bernadette, comes to his office. She tells him that people are angry about the closure, which he expected, and angry with him, which he did not. "They thought you were hiding," she says. "Were you?"

Ravi had been told by head office that he must read the statement exactly as written, for legal reasons. He took that to mean he must read it with his eyes on the page.

On the drive home that evening, he keeps hearing the shout from the back of the hall, and realises that he had not been able to see who had shouted, because he had not looked up.

Bernadette also tells him that a woman who has worked on the line for thirty years had said, "He couldn't even look at us." Ravi had sat beside that woman's husband at the plant's last Christmas dinner.
moreCases.misread:
The workforce read Ravi's grip on the lectern, his lowered eyes and his reading voice as a man hiding behind a statement, unwilling to face them. Ravi read his own manner as the proper, careful way to deliver an official announcement.

Ravi also read the silence after his statement as the workforce having nothing to say, when it was shock, and the first question came out as anger because nobody had been looked at.

Bernadette, too, had at first read his manner as hiding, until she remembered the months he had spent arguing with head office on the plant's behalf.
moreCases.betterRead:
A lectern gripped with both hands becomes a barrier, and a speaker reading with his eyes down disappears behind it. On a day of bad news, that reads as hiding, however it is meant. The chapter on the poker face earlier in this part described how a face that shows nothing when delivering bad news is read as indifference. Ravi's better approach, which Bernadette suggested, was a second meeting. This time he stepped out from behind the lectern and stood still in front of it, without notes for the first part. He looked at people, one face at a time, said that he was sorry, that he had argued against the decision and lost, and that he would do everything he could for each of them. He let the silence after that sit. Then he took questions, turning to each person who asked. People were still angry, but several came up afterwards to shake his hand.

He also read the legally required statement at the end, slowly, looking up after each paragraph.

workedReading.title: Giving a talk when the slides fail
workedReading.scene:
Naomi, thirty-nine, is a transport planner, and she is giving a fifteen-minute talk at a regional planning conference about a bus scheme her council has introduced. It is the first time she has spoken to an audience of more than a hundred. She has prepared well: a page of headings, a set of slides with maps and charts, and an opening and closing she knows by heart. She has rehearsed aloud, standing, four times, and once in front of a colleague. She is speaking third in the morning session, in a hotel conference room with a small stage, a lectern to one side and a large screen. She arrives forty minutes early to look at the room. She knows that nothing in her preparation will stop her heart pounding in the wings.

Her colleague, watching her rehearsal, gave her one piece of advice: "Don't let the slides give the talk. You give the talk." Naomi wrote it on the back of her headings page without quite knowing why.

steps.label: Walk the stage first
steps.text:
During the coffee break before the session, she walks onto the empty stage, stands where she will stand, and looks out at the room. She notices where the lectern is, where the screen is, and where the steps are. She finds two places she can move between for her transitions. Seeing the room from the stage takes away some of the strangeness, so that when she walks on later, it will be a place she has stood.

She also checks the practical things: where to put her water, whether the microphone clips on or is handheld, and how to get from her seat to the stage without climbing over anyone's bag.

She also sits for a minute in a seat at the back, to see how far away the stage looks and how large she will need to make her gestures.

steps.label: Run the wings routine
steps.text:
While the second speaker is finishing, she stands at the side of the room. Her heart is racing. She says under her breath, "I am excited," which feels slightly silly, and remembers that Brooks found it worked better than trying to calm down. She takes three slow breaths with a long exhale, lets her shoulders drop and her hands hang loose, and reminds herself that her nerves are far less visible than they feel.

She also avoids looking at her phone in the last ten minutes, as the chapter on power posing suggests, and stands rather than sitting hunched in her seat.

steps.label: Pause before the first sentence
steps.text:
She walks on at an ordinary pace, stands in the centre of the stage, plants her feet and looks at the audience for two seconds before she speaks. Then she says her first sentence, which she knows by heart, to one woman in the third row. She pauses after it. The pause feels long to her. To the room, it feels like someone about to say something worth hearing.

She speaks her second sentence to a man near the back, and her third to a woman on the far side. Each thought goes to one person, and the room, watching her speak to them, feels spoken to as well.

steps.label: When the slides fail
steps.text:
Three minutes in, the screen goes blue. The technician waves an apologetic hand and starts fiddling with a laptop. Naomi feels a jolt of panic. Then she remembers that the talk is in her, not in the slides. She steps away from the dead screen, towards the audience, and says, "Well, you'll have to imagine the map. Picture a town with one main road and every bus stuck on it." People laugh.

She also resists the urge to apologise, beyond a single wry line. The audience does not need to manage her disappointment about the slides; they need the talk.

steps.label: Let the hands do the work
steps.text:
Without the map, she draws the town in the air with her hands: the main road, the new bus lane, the side streets the buses used to use. She has not planned any of it. Goldin-Meadow's work suggests that her hands are helping her think as well as helping the audience see. She moves a few steps for each new section and stands still for each key result, which she gives to one face, then another.

She notices, a few minutes in, that she has stopped thinking about her nerves altogether. Explaining the town with her hands has taken all her attention, which is perhaps why it works.

Her movement also gives the room something to follow while the screen is dead: a step to the left for the old routes, a step to the right for the new.

steps.label: Take the questions well
steps.text:
The slides come back just in time for her closing chart, and she uses it briefly, then turns back to the room. For questions, she steps forward, turns her body to each person who asks, listens without nodding through their words, pauses before she answers, and ends each answer by looking back at the questioner. One question she cannot answer. She says so, and offers to find out.

A man at the back asks a sharp question about cost. She turns to him, keeps her face attentive, gives the figure and the reason for it, and looks back at him at the end. He nods.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Afterwards, several people tell her that the talk was the best of the morning, and two mention the drawing in the air. The session chair says that the slide failure was the best thing that could have happened to her talk. Naomi is not sure about that. She is sure that her preparation, aloud and on her feet, is what let her keep going when the screen went blue, and she writes "rehearse without slides once" at the top of her checklist for next time.

She also notices, watching the recording later, that her voice wobbled in the first minute, which she had felt intensely, and that on the recording it is barely audible.

She also realises that she never once thought about the woman in the third row's expression after the first sentence.

moreFailures.title: Announcing your nerves
moreFailures.body:
Many nervous speakers begin by saying so: "I'm not very good at this," "Bear with me, I'm really nervous," or a string of apologies when the voice wobbles. It feels honest, and it is sometimes meant to win sympathy. Usually it backfires. The illusion of transparency means that most of what you feel is invisible from the seats, and announcing it makes the audience look for it, so that a shake they would never have noticed becomes the thing they watch. It also frames the talk as an ordeal you are getting through rather than something you have come to give them. If your voice wobbles, pause, breathe out and carry on. If you need a moment, take it without explanation; a pause reads as composure. An audience that has not been told you are nervous will mostly assume you are not.

It is fine to acknowledge something the audience can plainly see, such as a cough or a dropped card, with a light word. Then move on.

moreFailures.title: Talking to the slides
moreFailures.body:
A common habit, especially for speakers who are nervous or who know their slides better than their talk, is to turn towards the screen and read it, sometimes for minutes at a time. The audience sees the speaker's back or side, the voice is directed away from them, and their eyes follow the speaker's gaze to the screen, so that nobody is looking at anybody. It also tends to slow the talk to the pace of reading. If you need to point something out on a slide, turn to it briefly, point, then turn back to the room before you speak about it. Keep a small copy of your slides or your headings on the lectern or a monitor in front of you, so that you can glance down rather than turning round. Slides should support the talk, not become the person the audience watches.

A remote clicker helps, because it lets you change slides without turning towards the laptop as well as the screen.

moreFailures.title: Rehearsing only in your head
moreFailures.body:
Many people prepare a talk by reading it over silently or running through it in their heads on the train, as Sam did. It feels like rehearsal, but it leaves out almost everything that happens on the day: the voice, the breath, the pace, the hands, the moment when you have to find your place without stopping. Speaking aloud is slower than thinking, and a talk timed in your head will usually run long or, under nerves, get rushed. The body also needs to learn the talk. Rehearse aloud, standing, at least several times, ideally in a space like the one you will use, and at least once in front of someone. Record one run and listen to it. The first time you hear your talk aloud should not be in front of the audience.

Rehearse the transitions between sections more than the sections themselves, because that is where speakers most often lose their way.

moreFailures.title: Taking faces in the audience as verdicts
moreFailures.body:
From a stage, individual faces can look alarming. A man in the second row frowns, a woman checks her phone, someone yawns, and a nervous speaker reads each one as a judgment and starts to shrink or speed up. But most faces in an audience are resting faces, and a listening face often looks serious, even stern. A frown may be concentration, a phone may be a note being taken, a yawn may be an early start. The chapters on reading in Part I warned against reading single signals in isolation, and the warning applies doubly from a stage, where you have no baseline for anyone. Find a few responsive faces, by all means, and speak some thoughts to them. But do not let one face write your review. Look at the whole room over the whole talk, and judge it afterwards, if at all, by what people say and ask.

If you want honest feedback, ask two or three people afterwards what they remember. That is a better verdict than any face in the second row.

questions.q: What should I do with my hands while I speak?
questions.a:
Mostly, let them do what they do when you explain something to a friend. Goldin-Meadow and colleagues found that gesturing lightens the mental load of explaining, so pinning your hands to your sides or holding them rigidly can make speaking harder. When you are not gesturing, let them rest at your sides or lightly together in front of you, at about waist height, rather than in your pockets, clasped tightly or fiddling with a pen. If your hands shake, rest them on the lectern for a moment, or hold a single card. Avoid scripting gestures to particular lines, which tends to look wooden. If you want to check your hands, record yourself explaining something you care about and watch with the sound off.

And if you hold something, such as a clicker or a single card, hold it lightly in one hand so that the other is free.

If you notice a habit you dislike, such as touching your face, replace it with something simple, such as resting your hands together, rather than trying to stop it by force.

Memorise the beginning and the end, and keep the middle as headings. Knowing your first sentence or two by heart gets you through the moment when nerves are highest, and knowing your last sentence means you can finish cleanly rather than trailing off. For the middle, a script learned word for word tends to sound recited, and if you lose a word you can lose your place entirely. Headings let you speak the content in your own words, which sounds more natural and is easier to recover if you stumble. The exception is a talk where precise wording matters, such as a formal statement or a tribute, where reading carefully, with pauses and frequent looks up, is perfectly acceptable.

Put your headings in large type, so that a glance is enough to find your place.

Whatever you choose, rehearse with exactly the notes you will use on the day, so that your eyes know where to find things.

questions.q: What if my mind goes blank in the middle?
questions.a:
Pause, breathe out and look at your notes. A pause of several seconds feels endless to you and ordinary to the audience, who mostly assume you are thinking, which you are. If the next point does not come, go back to the last thing you said and summarise it in a sentence, which often brings the thread back. If it still does not come, say plainly, "Let me check where I am," and look at your headings. Speakers lose their place far more often than audiences realise, and the ones who recover calmly are remembered as composed. What makes a blank feel like a disaster is the panic around it, and the routine of pause, breath, notes and summary gives the panic something to do.

Many experienced speakers keep a single line at the top of their notes, the main point of the talk, for exactly this moment.

questions.q: Does saying "I am excited" really work, and what if it feels silly?
questions.a:
In Brooks's study, people who said "I am excited" before a speech gave talks that independent viewers rated as more persuasive, competent and confident than people who said "I am calm", though they did not necessarily feel less anxious. The idea is that anxiety and excitement feel physically similar, and naming the feeling as excitement turns attention towards what might go well. Feeling silly is fine and may even help, because a small laugh at yourself loosens the body. If the word does not fit the occasion, such as a difficult announcement, a phrase such as "I'm ready" may suit you better, though Brooks tested excitement, not other phrases. The point is to reinterpret the arousal, not to fight it.

Combine it with slow breathing, which settles the body while the reappraisal settles the mind.

Some people find that saying it aloud, even quietly, works better than thinking it.

questions.q: How should I handle questions after a talk?
questions.a:
Treat each question as a conversation with one person, held in front of the room. Turn your body and your face to the person asking, and listen to the whole question without nodding through it or starting to answer in your head. Pause briefly before you reply, which shows that you are thinking about their question rather than reciting an answer. Begin your answer to the questioner, then widen it to the room, and end it by looking back at the questioner, which signals that you have finished. If you do not know the answer, say so and offer to find out. If a question is hostile, keep your voice level and your face attentive, answer the substance and do not get drawn into a duel.

If there is no roaming microphone, repeat or summarise the question for the room, so that everyone knows what you are answering.

questions.q: Does any of this apply to presentations on video?
questions.a:
Much of it does, with some changes. The chapters on the video call body and camera height earlier in this part describe the setup: camera at eye level, head and shoulders in the frame, good light and a good microphone. On video, the lens is your audience, so for your key points, look into the lens rather than at the faces on the screen. Many people present better standing, even on video, because it frees the breath and the hands; raise the camera to match. Pauses matter even more, because of the delay. And the wings routine still helps: a few slow breaths, a word of reappraisal and a moment to look at the lens before you begin.

If you can, ask someone else to watch the chat or the questions, so that you can keep your attention on the lens and the talk.

And if you present on video often, record one session and watch it back, as the chapter on video review in Part VI describes.

watch.title: Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford Commencement Address
watch.notice: A speech read from notes, with few gestures and no stagecraft. Notice how much presence comes from content and conviction rather than performance.

reviewPrompt: Before your next talk, say I am excited and take two slow breaths, then let your hands move and pause before your key point.
